stories.title: Born in New York, June 19, 1903
stories.text: Henry Louis Gehrig was born on June 19, 1903, in New York City. The boy the world would come to know as Lou grew up to play first base for the Yankees.

stories.title: 2,130 games in a row
stories.text: Lou Gehrig played in 2,130 consecutive games for the New York Yankees. Day after day, season after season, his name was in the lineup.

stories.title: The 1934 Triple Crown
stories.text: In 1934 Lou Gehrig led the American League in batting average, home runs and runs batted in, baseball's Triple Crown. He hit .363 with 49 home runs and 166 runs batted in. It was a remarkable season.

stories.title: The numbers behind the legend
stories.text: Over his career Lou Gehrig hit 493 home runs, drove in 1,995 runs and batted .340. He did it in 17 seasons, all with the Yankees. The Baseball Hall of Fame calls him one of the most magnificent hitters and run producers in history.

stories.title: Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day, July 4, 1939
stories.text: On July 4, 1939, the Yankees held Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day at Yankee Stadium. Speaking to the crowd, Gehrig said he considered himself the luckiest man on the face of the earth.

stories.title: How Lou Gehrig took over first base
stories.text: In 1925 the Yankees already had a first baseman, Wally Pipp. After Pipp sat out a game with a headache, Gehrig played first base, and he kept the job. He would go on to play every game there for the Yankees until 1939.

stories.title: Named Yankees captain in 1935
stories.text: On April 21, 1935, manager Joe McCarthy named Lou Gehrig captain of the Yankees. Gehrig was not sure he was the right man, because he did not think of himself as a vocal leader. He held the title until his death in 1941.

stories.title: Lou Gehrig on the All-Century Team
stories.text: In 1999 Major League Baseball named its All-Century Team. Lou Gehrig was the leading vote-getter, and he was named the team's starting first baseman.

stories.title: A home run in the 1937 All-Star Game
stories.text: In the 1937 All-Star Game at Griffith Stadium in Washington, Lou Gehrig hit a home run off National League starter Dizzy Dean, giving the American League a 2-0 lead. The American League went on to win. The game is also remembered for the injury Dean suffered in the same inning.

stories.title: Two cycles
stories.text: Lou Gehrig hit for the cycle twice: on June 25, 1934, against the White Sox, and again on August 1, 1937. A cycle means a single, a double, a triple and a home run in one game.

stories.title: A scout sees Columbia's Lou Gehrig
stories.text: In April 1923 Yankees scout Paul Krichell went to watch Columbia play Rutgers. Gehrig hit two home runs, and Krichell was so impressed that he phoned Yankees general manager Ed Barrow to say he had found another Babe Ruth.

stories.title: Lou marries Eleanor Twitchell
stories.text: Lou Gehrig met Eleanor Twitchell, a secretary from Chicago, at a party, and they stayed in touch mostly by letter. He proposed after the Yankees came to Chicago in May 1933, and they were married on September 29, 1933.

stories.title: Gehrig's Larrupin' Lous against Ruth's Bustin' Babes
stories.text: After the 1927 season, Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig set out on a three-week barnstorming tour. Each captained a team of local players: Gehrig's team was the Larrupin' Lous and Ruth's was the Bustin' Babes. More than 250,000 fans came out to see them.

stories.title: Why Lou Gehrig wore number 4
stories.text: Lou Gehrig wore uniform number 4 because he batted behind Babe Ruth, the third hitter in the Yankees' lineup.

stories.text: In 1969 the Baseball Writers' Association of America voted Lou Gehrig the greatest first baseman of all time.

stories.title: Joe DiMaggio arrives, 1936
stories.text: In 1936 Joe DiMaggio joined the Yankees. The 21-year-old had already drawn national attention in the Pacific Coast League, and the New York press called him the replacement for Babe Ruth. Gehrig praised the newcomer.
